strengths: FaceXFormer addresses a useful computer vision problem: integrating nine heterogeneous facial analysis tasks into one shared model. Combining dense parsing, landmarks, pose, and classification outputs could simplify deployment and annotation without requiring the best score on every task.

The reported results are competitive across several benchmarks, including 3.52° MAE on BIWI, 3.05 NME on the full 300W set, and 91.83% attribute accuracy on CelebA. The cross-dataset improvement on challenging 300VW Category C—6.75 NME versus STARLoss's 8.42—is particularly encouraging.

The architectural overview is understandable. The four-backbone comparison and supplementary component ablations provide initial evidence for the design choices, while the appendix documents dataset characteristics and augmentation settings.
The manuscript usefully acknowledges retraining requirements, data imbalance, and qualitative age/race prediction failures. These limitations help define the contribution's practical scope.
weaknesses: The decoder's novelty and benefits are insufficiently established. Its alternating task/image attention and final token-to-image attention closely resemble SAM's two-way decoder [34], but this relationship is not explained in the method. Task tokens also appear in Faceptor/QFace. Table C.1 removes the entire decoder or multiscale features; it does not compare against a standard decoder or shared-backbone task heads under matched training. Single-task versus joint-training controls are also needed to substantiate positive transfer.

Training and evaluation ambiguities affect reproducibility and interpretation. Loss weights and missing-label handling are unspecified, and the additional three training epochs 'for some tasks' leave unclear whether all headline task results come from one checkpoint. Appendix E.5 introduces MORPH-II training/evaluation beyond the main protocol and UTKFace results. Exact splits and overlap exclusions for related datasets such as CelebA/CelebAMask-HQ and 300W/300W-LP are needed to assess evaluation independence.

The claimed resolution of conflicting preprocessing requirements is not demonstrated quantitatively. Section 3.4 motivates the conflict between landmark alignment and pose estimation, yet Appendix E.2 aligns landmark images using five points while E.3 loosely crops pose images. A common inference preprocessing pipeline and coordinate convention should be specified and evaluated across tasks.

A prominent numerical result requires correction or explanation: Table 2's ten FaceXFormer class scores average to 91.01, rather than the reported 92.01. Using those values, the advantage over Faceptor's 90.89 is 0.12 points instead of 1.12. This preserves competitiveness but substantially changes the claimed improvement. Section 4.3 also calls 4.67 the mean landmark NME, although Table 4 assigns it to the challenging subset; the full-set value is 3.05.

Efficiency is central to the contribution but inadequately validated. Table 5 reports 109.29M parameters and 33.21 FPS without an explicit inference hardware, batch-size, precision, or timing protocol. There are no comparable runtime measurements against existing unified models or a collection of specialized models, and decoder costs are not isolated. Consequently, the claimed parameter-efficiency advantage remains uncertain.

Evaluation does not fully support the breadth of the generalization claims. No quantitative race-prediction result is provided, and the LFWA evaluation in Table B.1 covers only gender rather than the full attribute task. Appendix D's qualitative examples come from CelebAMask-HQ, a training domain of the shared encoder, so they provide limited evidence of out-of-distribution robustness.

The claim of minimal bias exceeds Table 6's evidence. Combining six racial categories into one 'Non-white' group can conceal subgroup disparities. The age discrepancy of 0.50 is larger than CLIP's absolute 0.30 and FaRL's 0.35, so the smallest-gap claim holds only for gender. Attributing reduced bias to race co-training also requires an ablation. The proposed surveillance and annotation applications warrant discussion of how demographic prediction errors could propagate.
